items.title: Going further: how the tracker is tested, and the same rules in Express
items.body:
The later questions use two more lessons.

1. **astraupskill/04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md** explains what the Java regression suite checks, how its assertions are written, how to investigate a failing save or update, and why a second set of CLI scenarios exists. Read the opening paragraphs first, then the section on reproducing the CLI scenarios and the two notes that follow it.
2. **astraupskill/08-SAME-RULES-IN-EXPRESS.md** rebuilds one update path in TypeScript, Express and SQLite. Read the sketch slowly, then the Mapping table (each Java idea next to its web equivalent), then the table of places where the port behaves differently from the Java CLI.

As you read the port, keep asking one question for every row: is this really the same rule, or only something that looks like it? The lesson itself answers that question for some inputs.

excerpts.quote: "The rules do not change" is the goal, but the sketch above changes four of them.

items.title: The web boundary meets inputs the CLI never could
items.body:
The CLI asks for fixed fields one prompt at a time, so it can never send an unexpected field. A web client can send any JSON it likes. That is why the mapping row for parseAmount and parseDate adds .strict() to the body schema: unknown fields are refused instead of silently ignored or passed along.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- The schema does trim title and category, but that is not the rule the mapping row adds.
- The 500-character note cap exists in the schema, but it is not the highlighted difference.
- The note default exists too; the mapping row is about unknown fields.

A strict boundary keeps the port's rules as narrow as the CLI's.

excerpts.quote: `.strict()` refuses unknown fields the CLI could never send

items.title: Why both labels group as Income Tax under a Turkish locale
items.body:
**Key: one entry, Income Tax, holding both amounts, because case conversion uses Locale.ROOT.**

Expense.normalizeCategory trims the text, splits it on runs of whitespace, then upper-cases the first letter and lower-cases the rest of each word with Locale.ROOT. Both " INCOME   tax " and "income tax" become "Income Tax", so getSpendingByCategory adds them under one key. Locale.ROOT matters because Turkish case rules map i and I to dotted and dotless forms; the regression test sets tr-TR on purpose to prove the label does not change.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Two entries because of inner spaces**: the split on whitespace runs collapses them before the words are joined with single spaces.
- **INCOME TAX**: the policy is title case, not upper case.
- **Dotless Turkish i**: that would happen only with the default locale; the code passes Locale.ROOT explicitly.

excerpts.quote: result.append(word.substring(0, 1).toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT)); result.append(word.substring(1).toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT));
category normalization is shared and locale independent

items.title: Why the corrupt fixture fails on line 3
items.body:
The loader reports errors by physical line number in the file. The fixture starts with a header comment on line 1, has a good record on line 2, and the bad record sits on line 3, so that is the number in the message. Comment lines count like any other line.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- The count is not by records; if it were, the bad record would be the second, not the third.
- The parser does not read ahead and report the following line.
- Numbering starts at 1, with the header comment as line 1.

When you debug a load error, open the file and count physical lines, header included.

excerpts.quote: because the header comment is line 1 and line numbers count every physical line

items.title: Why a deleted highest id comes back after a restart
items.body:
**Key: the new expense gets #2, because nextId is rebuilt from the highest id still in the file.**

During a session ExpenseManager keeps nextId in memory, so deleting #2 and adding again in the same session would give #3. But nothing writes nextId to disk. On startup loadExpenses scans the loaded records, finds the highest id (1, because #2 was deleted and saved away) and sets nextId to that plus one. So #2 is issued again. 02-CONCEPTS names this limit, and practice exercise 4 is about fixing it.

Why the others are wrong:
- **#3 from a counter in the file header**: the header save writes is a fixed column list; it holds no counter.
- **#3 from a tombstone list**: there is no record of deleted ids anywhere.
- **#1 after a reset to one**: loadExpenses always recomputes nextId from the loaded ids, so it never restarts at one while #1 exists.

excerpts.quote: nextId = highestId == Long.MAX_VALUE ? 0 : highestId + 1;
A deleted highest ID can therefore be reused across sessions

items.title: The port's regex refuses a trailing zero
items.body:
The sketch's money schema starts with a regex that allows at most two decimals, so 12.300 fails validation and the request gets a 400 before any conversion happens. The lesson records the fix: allow any number of decimals in the regex, then reject only non-zero third decimals, so trailing zeros pass.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- The regex fails first, so the cents transform never runs.
- The dot is not ignored, and BigInt is the fix for a different row.
- The schema returns 400, not 422, and the refine is not where it fails.

excerpts.quote: 400, because the regex allows only 1-2 decimals

items.title: The port trims a category but never normalizes it
items.body:
The sketch declares the category as z.string().trim().min(1).max(60). Trim removes the spaces around ' TRAVEL ', and that is all: zod's string helpers do not change letter case, so the row stores TRAVEL. The lesson lists this among the four places where the port quietly changes a rule, and its fix is a .transform() that normalizes the category the same way the Java constructor does.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- Trim only removes whitespace; it never capitalizes anything.
- The category is trimmed exactly like the title.
- The schema has no list of allowed categories, so any non-empty text up to 60 characters passes.

A translation is only the same rule if every normalization step comes with it.

excerpts.quote: category: z.string().trim().min(1).max(60)

items.title: How the manager refuses to wrap ids past Long.MAX_VALUE
items.body:
**Key: the first add gets Long.MAX_VALUE, and the second throws IllegalStateException.**

After loading id Long.MAX_VALUE - 1, nextId is Long.MAX_VALUE, so the first add uses it. addExpense then advances nextId with a guard: if it just used Long.MAX_VALUE, it stores the sentinel 0 instead of adding one. The next call sees nextId == 0 and throws "Expense id space is exhausted." before touching the list. The regression test "exhausted identity never wraps to negative" checks both calls and that the list still has two entries.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Long.MIN_VALUE after overflow**: plain long arithmetic would wrap, which is exactly what the sentinel prevents; Expense also rejects ids that are not positive.
- **Reuses id 1**: there is no free-id search.
- **Ids above Integer.MAX_VALUE rejected**: ids are long values; the constructor only requires id > 0.

excerpts.quote: if (nextId == 0) throw new IllegalStateException("Expense id space is exhausted.");
nextId = nextId == Long.MAX_VALUE ? 0 : nextId + 1;

items.title: Why 12.300 is accepted and stored as 12.30
items.body:
**Key: it is accepted and stored as 12.30, because dropping a trailing zero needs no rounding.**

parseAmount builds new BigDecimal(value) and then calls setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY). UNNECESSARY means "change the scale only if the numeric value stays exactly the same, otherwise throw ArithmeticException". 12.300 and 12.30 are the same number, so the call succeeds. 1.001 would need rounding, so it throws and becomes "Amount must use at most 2 decimal places."

Why the others are wrong:
- **Rejected for the third digit**: the rule is about value-changing digits, not the count of digits typed. 02-CONCEPTS uses exactly this example.
- **Stored as 12.300**: setScale returns a new BigDecimal at scale 2; that is what the Expense holds.
- **Rounded half-up with a warning**: no rounding mode other than UNNECESSARY is used, and nothing prints a warning.

excerpts.quote: new BigDecimal(value).setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY)
is accepted because reducing its scale to two requires no rounding

items.title: One difference where the port is right and Java should change
items.body:
Most rows of the differences table fix the port to match the Java CLI. The 1e2 row runs the other way: the port's 400 is the behaviour the lesson wants to keep, because practice exercise 2 asks the Java code to accept plain decimals only.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- The Java side is not the reference for this row; it is the side being changed.
- Accepting scientific notation everywhere is the opposite of exercise 2.
- The input is reachable: a user can type it into the CLI today.

So matching rules can mean changing either side, as long as the decision is written down.

excerpts.quote: keep the port's behavior; it is what practice exercise 2 asks of Java

items.title: Why typing YES in capitals confirms a delete
items.body:
**Key: the expense is removed, because the answer is compared with equalsIgnoreCase.**

deleteExpenseFlow reads the id, checks the expense exists, then prompts "Type yes to confirm" and tests the reply with equalsIgnoreCase("yes"). YES, Yes and yes all pass; anything else, such as y or no, prints "Deletion cancelled." Only then does it call deleteExpense, which removes the entry from the in-memory list. Running the CLI with YES piped in removes the record.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Only lowercase yes**: equalsIgnoreCase ignores letter case.
- **The prompt repeats**: there is no loop; one non-matching answer cancels and returns to the menu.
- **The file is rewritten at once**: deleteExpense only changes the list. The file is written by the save at the end of the session.

excerpts.quote: .equalsIgnoreCase("yes")
return expenses.removeIf(expense -> expense.getId() == id);

items.title: What object-level tests cannot see, and how the CLI scenarios fill the gap
items.body:
The 23 Java tests construct managers and storage objects directly. That makes them fast and precise, but they never type into the menu, never restart the process, and never see standard input end in the middle of a command. The lesson therefore re-creates five cross-process scenarios as a node --test file that uses the practice harness to compile the app into a temp directory and run the real CLI against a temp data file.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- The Java suite does exercise storage, with real temporary files.
- Operating systems and CI speed are not the reason given.
- The scenarios run under node --test, not a PowerShell replay, Docker or parallel JUnit.

excerpts.quote: The Java suite builds objects directly, so it never checks the menu, process restarts, or EOF handling.

items.title: Why the day check needs its second half
items.body:
JavaScript's date parser is lenient: given 2026-02-30 it does not fail, it rolls the extra days into March and returns a valid timestamp for 2026-03-02. So !Number.isNaN(Date.parse(s)) alone would let an impossible date through. The sketch's refine adds a second test, new Date(s).toISOString().startsWith(s): the rolled-over date prints as 2026-03-02T00:00:00.000Z, which does not start with 2026-02-30, so the value is refused. A month of 13 fails earlier, because Date.parse returns NaN for it.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- The regex only checks the digit pattern; it knows nothing about month lengths.
- Date.parse returns a number here, not NaN (checked with Node v22.16.0).
- toISOString does not throw for a rolled-over date.

The round trip back to text is what turns a lenient parser into a strict check.

excerpts.quote: new Date(s).toISOString().startsWith(s), 'Date must be a real calendar day.'

items.title: Why an invalid save cannot damage the existing file
items.body:
**Key: the file stays byte for byte the same, because validation throws before any temp file exists.**

save first copies the list, then runs it through a fresh ExpenseManager's loadExpenses. That method throws IllegalArgumentException on a duplicate id. Only after validation and serialization does save create the temporary sibling and write it, and only after that does Files.move replace the target. So a duplicate never reaches the disk. The test "invalid save preserves existing bytes" reads the file before and after and compares the strings.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Cut down to the header**: that was the old behaviour when a writer opened the destination first; the worked change removed it.
- **Only the first record**: nothing de-duplicates; the duplicate rejects the whole save.
- **Both records, rejected on next load**: the duplicate check runs inside save itself, so such a file is never written.

excerpts.quote: List<Expense> snapshot = List.copyOf(expenses); var validator = new ExpenseManager(); validator.loadExpenses(snapshot);
invalid save preserves existing bytes

items.title: 428, 409 or 404: how the sketched PUT reads a zero-row update
items.body:
The handler requires If-Match: if the header is missing or not an integer it answers 428 and asks for the version the client loaded. The UPDATE then includes WHERE id = ? AND version = ?. When it changes no rows, there are two possible reasons, so the handler runs a SELECT: if the row exists the version was stale (409), otherwise the id is unknown (404). A successful update returns 204 with the moved ETag.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- A missing header is not treated as version 1, and not every zero-row result is a 409.
- It is a 428, not a 400, and nothing is retried.
- The check is never skipped, and zero changes is never reported as success.

excerpts.quote: if (!Number.isInteger(expected)) return res.status(428)
? res.status(409).json({ error: 'Expense changed since you loaded it. Reload and retry.' })

items.title: Core idea: the live list in memory versus the file on disk
items.body:
Two copies of the data exist while the app runs: the live list inside ExpenseManager, and the text file written by ExpenseFileStorage. Most reliability questions in this course are about the gap between them.

Trace App.run from top to bottom and mark three things: where the file is loaded, where the menu loop runs, and where the save is called. Then list every way a session can end (a refused load, choosing 7, input running out) and follow each path to see which code it reaches.

Next, learn the file format: one line per expense, fields separated by tabs, with escape sequences so a tab or newline inside a field cannot split a record. Compare load with save line by line. Which lines does load treat as records, and what exactly does save write back? In save, write down the order of its steps before you read the worked change.

excerpts.quote: A copied list is a collection snapshot, not a durable commit.
public class ExpenseFileStorage {

readMore.why: run, loadExpenses and saveExpenses are the whole lifecycle of a session.
The worked change explains three fixes to load and save in turn.

items.title: What a refused startup does, including its exit status
items.body:
**Key: the CLI prints the load error, skips the menu and the save, and exits with status 0.**

The third line of the record cannot be parsed, so ExpenseFileStorage.load throws IOException and App.loadExpenses prints "Could not load saved expenses: ..." and returns false. run then returns at its first line, before the try/finally that holds the save, so the file is not touched. main has nothing more to do and ends normally, so the JVM exits 0. The trace lab shows $LASTEXITCODE printing 0.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Skips line 3 and opens the menu**: load rejects the whole file on any bad record; it never returns a partial list.
- **Exit code 1**: nothing calls System.exit; that gap is practice exercise 3.
- **Empty menu, then overwrite**: the early return happens before the menu loop and before the save, which is the point of the fix.

excerpts.quote: if (!loadExpenses()) return;
Now look at the `$LASTEXITCODE` line: it prints `0`.

items.title: The test harness is a contract, not a framework
items.body:
The tracker's tests run through a tiny named-test wrapper: each check prints PASS or FAIL and the run exits nonzero if any check fails. There is no Maven, Gradle, JUnit, network or database. The lesson treats that observable behaviour as the contract: if the project later moves to a real test framework, the migration should keep those checks of behaviour rather than switch to assertions about private implementation details.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- There is no JUnit, Maven or coverage report to preserve.
- Checking private fields is exactly what the lesson warns against.
- No Gradle or database is involved; the harness needs neither.

excerpts.quote: prints PASS or FAIL, and exits nonzero if any check fails
A future test-framework migration should preserve these contracts rather than replace them with assertions about private implementation details.

items.title: A confirmation prompt has no server-side equivalent
items.body:
The CLI asks the user to confirm before deleting. A server cannot depend on that: it has no idea whether any client showed a prompt, and a script can call DELETE directly. So the mapping table maps the prompt to nothing and puts authorization in its place: the server decides whether this caller may delete, not whether they clicked twice.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- The sketched DELETE route takes no confirmation parameter.
- A second request is not treated as confirmation.
- DELETE in the sketch sends no If-Match header, and a header could not prove a prompt was shown.

excerpts.quote: nothing: the server cannot rely on a client prompt; authorization goes here instead

items.title: Core idea: where the rules live and how text becomes values
items.body:
An invariant is a rule that every accepted record must satisfy. This project keeps its rules in two layers, and it helps to know which layer you are reading.

1. **The Expense constructor** runs for every record, whether it came from the menu or from the saved file.
2. **The manager's parsers** (parseAmount, parseDate, parseYearMonth, normalizeCategory) turn the raw strings a user typed into BigDecimal, LocalDate and a clean category label.

A useful exercise: for each parser, write down what text it accepts, what it rejects, and which message the user sees. Do not guess from the method name. Check the JDK call each parser delegates to (the BigDecimal string constructor, setScale with a RoundingMode, LocalDate.parse) and what that call accepts or throws. For categories, note how words are split and which Locale the case conversion uses.

Then read the regression tests that start with "domain", "invalid" and "category" and match each one to the layer that rejects or reshapes the input.

excerpts.quote: An invariant is a rule that must hold for every accepted state.
private BigDecimal parseAmount(String amountText)

readMore.why: The constructor and normalizeCategory: the rules every record passes through.

items.title: Why a rejected update leaves the old expense untouched
items.body:
**Key: Lunch stays at 12.30 with its old note, because the call throws before expenses.set.**

updateExpense finds the index, then builds a complete replacement Expense. Building it calls parseAmount and parseDate. LocalDate.parse rejects 2026-02-30, so parseDate throws IllegalArgumentException and the next line, expenses.set(i, replacement), never runs. Because Expense is immutable and the list entry was never replaced, every field and every total is as before. The regression test "invalid update preserves previous value" checks the note and the total.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Bus with the old date**: there is no field-by-field update; the whole replacement is built first or not at all.
- **Clamped to 2026-02-28**: LocalDate.parse with the ISO format rejects a day that does not exist; it does not adjust it.
- **No expense #1**: nothing is removed; set replaces in place and is never reached.

excerpts.quote: Expense replacement = new Expense(id, title, parseAmount(amount), category, parseDate(date), note); expenses.set(i, replacement);
invalid update preserves previous value

items.title: Why a typed-over id prints the parser message
items.body:
**Key: "Could not update expense: For input string: \"abc\"".**

updateExpenseFlow reads the id with Long.parseLong(prompt("Expense id")) inside its try block. parseLong throws NumberFormatException for abc, and NumberFormatException is a subclass of IllegalArgumentException, so the flow catch handles it and prints "Could not update expense: " plus the JDK message. The id text is passed on untrimmed, so " 1" with a leading space fails the same way. Piping 8 then abc into the CLI prints exactly this line, and the menu returns.

Why the others are wrong:
- **"Expense id must be positive."**: that is the Expense constructor message, and no Expense is built because parsing fails first.
- **"Expense #abc does not exist."**: the existence check needs a long, so it runs only after parseLong succeeds.
- **"Invalid menu option."**: that message belongs to the menu switch; 8 was a valid choice and abc is read by the update flow.

excerpts.quote: long id = Long.parseLong(prompt("Expense id"));
} catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) { System.out.println("Could not update expense: " + ex.getMessage());

items.title: How trimming the line deleted expenses with empty notes
items.body:
**Key: line.trim() removed the trailing tab, so the parser saw five fields.**

A record is six tab-separated fields. When the note is empty, the line ends with a tab followed by nothing. That final tab is what makes the sixth field exist. The original loader trimmed the whole line before parsing, which removed the trailing tab, so the split produced five fields and the parser rejected the record. The old catch printed a message and carried on, so the list looked complete. The fix keeps trimming only for the blank/comment check and parses the original line.

Why the others are wrong:
- **toLine left out the note column**: the worked change shows the saved line still ends with the separating tab.
- **unescape returned null**: unescape builds a string; an empty field gives "".
- **The comment check matched**: comments are lines starting with #, and a record line starts with its id.

excerpts.quote: The old loader called `line.trim()` and passed that result into the parser. Trimming removed the trailing tab.
Expense expense = parseLine(line);

items.title: Why a hand-written comment line disappears after a session
items.body:
**Key: the file now holds the generated header and the records, and the user comment is gone.**

load skips any line whose trimmed text starts with #, so the comment is read and thrown away. It is never stored anywhere. When the session ends, run's finally block calls save even if nothing changed, and save always writes its own fixed header line followed by one line per expense. A save/load round trip in a scratch program shows the comment replaced by that header.

Why the others are wrong:
- **An unchanged session is not saved**: there is no dirty flag; every session that got past loading saves on the way out.
- **The comment kept above the header**: comments are not carried in memory, so save cannot write them back.
- **Loading fails on the comment line**: lines starting with # are skipped by design, not parsed.

excerpts.quote: if (trimmedLine.isEmpty() || trimmedLine.startsWith("#")) {
lines.add("# id\ttitle\tamount\tcategory\tdate\tnote");

items.title: Why typing 1e2 adds an expense of $100.00
items.body:
**Key: the expense shows $100.00, because new BigDecimal accepts scientific notation.**

parseAmount trims the text and hands it straight to the BigDecimal string constructor. That constructor accepts an optional sign and an exponent, so "1e2" is 100. setScale(2) then gives 100.00, which is positive, so every check passes. Running addExpense with "1e2" in a scratch program prints 100.00. The risk is real: a typo in an exponent changes an amount by orders of magnitude.

Why the others are wrong:
- **"Amount must be a valid number."**: that message appears only when BigDecimal throws NumberFormatException, and it does not throw for 1e2 (it does for "1_000").
- **$1.00, parsing stops at the e**: BigDecimal parses the whole string or throws; it never stops part-way.
- **Fails for having no decimal point**: whole numbers such as "12" are fine; setScale adds the two places.

excerpts.quote: BigDecimal amount = new BigDecimal(value).setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY);
String value = requireText(amountText, "Amount");

items.title: The atomic move becomes one statement in a transaction
items.body:
The Java store makes a save all-or-nothing by writing a temp file and moving it over the old one atomically. In the Express port, the single UPDATE statement runs inside SQLite's implicit transaction, which gives the same all-or-nothing effect for one row. If a change had to touch several rows, they would need an explicit BEGIN IMMEDIATE ... COMMIT around them.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- No temp table or RENAME is used.
- WAL checkpoints are not part of the design.
- A database file lock held until exit is not how the port achieves atomicity.

excerpts.quote: the single `UPDATE` inside SQLite's implicit transaction; several rows would be `BEGIN IMMEDIATE ... COMMIT`

items.title: Start here: four classes and the order to read the course
items.body:
This repo is a small Java 17 command-line expense tracker. Four classes do all the work:

- **App** - the menu, prompts and printed messages.
- **Expense** - one immutable expense (id, title, amount, category, date, note).
- **ExpenseManager** - the live list of expenses, id allocation, parsing of user text, totals.
- **ExpenseFileStorage** - turning the list into a text file and back.

Read the course in astraupskill/ in this order: the README (keep its glossary open), 01-CODEBASE-MAP, 02-CONCEPTS, 03-WORKED-CHANGE, 04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING and 07-TRACE-LAB. Leave 05-PRACTICE and 06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW until you have tried the exercises yourself.

You can compile and run the regression suite with nothing but a JDK: compile src and test into an out folder with javac, then run expensetracker.RegressionTests. Each test name describes one contract. When a guide and the code disagree, the code is the truth.

excerpts.quote: This course uses the four Java classes that actually run this project.
These constructor calls are a small composition root

readMore.why: Shows the plain javac/java commands for running the suite without PowerShell.
The 23 named regression tests; each name states one contract.

items.title: What gets saved when input ends in the middle of a command
items.body:
**Key: only the completed expense is saved, because the half-entered add never reached the manager.**

addExpenseFlow collects all five fields before it calls addExpense. When input ends during that collection, scanner.nextLine throws NoSuchElementException. run catches it, prints "Input ended. Saving completed changes.", and the finally block calls saveExpenses. The first add already sits in the live list, so it is written; the second never called the manager, so there is nothing to write. 04-TESTING re-creates this with a CLI test.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Nothing without option 7**: option 7 only ends the loop. Saving lives in finally, which runs on every exit from the try block.
- **Both, with defaults**: there are no default values; the add stopped before any Expense was built.
- **The exception skips the save**: run catches NoSuchElementException itself, and a finally block runs even when an exception is thrown.

excerpts.quote: catch (NoSuchElementException ex) { System.out.println("Input ended. Saving completed changes."); } finally { saveExpenses();
Fully completed changes are saved; a command interrupted halfway through collecting its fields has not yet called the manager.

items.title: Why a large amount lands one cent off in the port
items.body:
JavaScript numbers are doubles, which cannot represent every decimal exactly. The sketch converts the text to a Number and multiplies by 100, and for 90071992547409.99 the result rounds to 9007199254740998 cents: one cent wrong. The Java CLI uses BigDecimal and keeps the value exactly. The fix is to split the text on the dot and build the cent value with BigInt or integer string arithmetic, never through a double.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- The regex accepts the value with its two decimals; nothing is truncated there.
- SQLite integers are 64-bit, and REAL would make precision worse.
- The rounding function is not the cause; the error is already in the double.

excerpts.quote: one cent wrong, because `Number(s) * 100` goes through a double

items.title: A good failure test proves nothing else changed
items.body:
Expecting an exception only shows the bad call was refused. The lesson's update test goes further: after the rejected update it reads the existing expense and the running total again and checks that neither moved. The save and failed-move tests follow the same idea, comparing file bytes and checking that no temporary sibling leaked.

The lesson is also honest about the limit: these tests cover predictable filesystem failures, not a sudden machine power cut.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- The point is the surviving state, not the exception's message text.
- The test does not retry anything.
- Timing and full disks are not discussed.

excerpts.quote: It checks the failure and proves that existing state survived.
they do not emulate a sudden machine power cut
